channel.title: Ascentery blog
channel.description: Notes on Ascentery's text adventures and the talking avatar.

item.title: The Engine That Refuses to Die
item.description: A toolkit nobody advertises, a community that keeps shipping, and the quiet reason point-and-click games outlive their own obituaries.

item.title: Nobody Reads the Room Like a Badly Lit Room
item.description: The best adventure-game levels are badly lit rooms, and that's a compliment. Here's why not being able to see is the whole point.

item.title: Your Game Is Finished. Stop Touching It.
item.description: The last ten percent of a project eats the other ninety, and the only cure is a deadline you actually believe in.

item.title: Nostalgia Is a Loan the Adventure Game Has to Repay
item.description: Remakes and pixel art buy the genre attention and time. The question is whether it ever spends that on something it hasn't sold before.

item.title: The Scene Is a Series of Small Deadlines
item.description: Jams and demos don't die of bad ideas. They die of open-ended time. A look at the machinery that keeps adventure projects moving.

item.title: The Audience Didn't Shrink. It Got Absorbed.
item.description: Adventure games never lost their players so much as loaned them out, along with every trick the form invented.

item.title: The Best Item in the Game Is the One You Haven't Found
item.description: A comedy routine about inventory: a text adventure's real hero is the empty slot, and every item you pick up makes the game slightly worse.

item.title: The Line Is Short, and It Keeps Coming Back
item.description: Who actually shows up for text adventures, MUDs and roguelikes, why the queue stays modest, and why modest is not the same as empty.

item.title: Every Room Needs One Thing You Can't Use
item.description: Adventure games are hoarding simulators with a puzzle attached, and the junk you haul around is doing more work than the key.

item.title: Want to learn how to type fast on the keyboard? Forget typing apps, just play a command-input adventure games or MUD.
item.description: Typing drills are boring and you quit them. A text adventure gives your fingers somewhere to go, and the speed follows on its own.

item.title: The 80s Taught Players to Type at the Game
item.description: The parser era didn't fail because it was hard. It failed because it made players guess the machine's vocabulary instead of their own.

item.title: A Verb Is a Promise You Make to Yourself
item.description: The parser doesn't test your imagination. It tests whether you can bear to be told no by a machine you already know will say yes eventually.

item.title: Adventure Games in the 80s vs the 90s
item.description: Two decades, two ideas of what an adventure game owes the player: one demanded precision, the other offered comfort. Here's what each got right.

item.title: Adventure Games Are About Leaving Things Behind
item.description: The most useful thing an adventure game can teach you is when to stop picking things up, and almost none of them say so.

item.title: Errandale: A Walkthrough for the Unhurried
item.description: A step-by-step path through Errandale, plus a note on how 80s adventures punished and 90s adventures negotiated.

item.title: The Fae Grounds Paints a Garden You Never Noticed
item.description: Inside The Fae Grounds: how its painted garden, silver-green palette and quiet fae folklore turn an ordinary path into somewhere else.

item.title: A Failed Command Is the Game Talking Back
item.description: The parser's rejections are not obstacles between you and the story. They are the story, and the most honest part of the form.

item.title: A Locked Door Is a Question, Not a Wall
item.description: Adventure games don't block you with locked doors. They hand you a sentence you haven't finished yet.

item.title: A Walkthrough for The Last Delivery
item.description: A spoiler-warned, plain-English route through Ascentery's claymation morning: the bakery, the post office, the basement, and the town hall door.

item.title: The Mouse Hunt: Three Cheeses and a Sleeping Cat
item.description: A small mouse, a sleeping cat and three hidden cheeses. A warm introduction to The Mouse Hunt, a text adventure you play in the browser.
